items.prose: A firm's CV screener was trained on its past hires. Both groups have the same share of applicants who meet the job's stated requirements. The firm and the numbers are invented.

parts.question: What share of Group C does the screener shortlist? Give a percentage.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the shortlisted count by Group C's applicants.

byKey.of-all: You divided by all 200 applicants. The rate is out of Group C's 160.
byKey.count: You read the count, 56, as a percentage. Divide it by 160.

explain.text: $56 / 160 = 0.35$, so the screener shortlists 35% of Group C.

parts.question: Group C's rate is 35% from part 1. What share of Group D does it shortlist? Give a percentage.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the shortlisted count by Group D's applicants.

byKey.of-all: You divided by all 200 applicants. The rate is out of Group D's 40.
byKey.count: You read the count, 6, as a percentage. Divide it by 40.

explain.text: $6 / 40 = 0.15$, so the screener shortlists 15% of Group D.

parts.question: Using the rates from parts 1 and 2, how many percentage points apart are they?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract one rate from the other.

byKey.counts: You subtracted the counts, 56 − 6. The groups differ in size, so compare rates.
byKey.ratio: You divided the rates. The question asks how far apart they are.

explain.text: The rates are 35% and 15%, so they are 20 percentage points apart, though both groups meet the requirements in the same share.

parts.question: The firm judged its screener by "the shortlist looks like our past hires", when it wanted the people best able to do the job. Given the 20-point gap, which idea from l12 is this?

options.text: What was measured is not what was meant
The screener is not polite enough
options.why: Tone has nothing to do with it.

options.text: A bug in the screener's code
options.why: The code may work exactly as built. The measure is the problem.

options.text: No problem: matching past hires is the aim
options.why: The firm wanted the best candidates; matching the past was only its measure.

feedback.correct: Measured: looks like past hires. Meant: best able to do the job.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what was judged with what was wanted.

explain.text: The firm wanted the best candidates and measured likeness to past hires. The screener met the measure, gap included. That is the alignment gap of l12, met in bias from data.

items.prose: The same firm retrains its screener on who met the job's stated requirements, not on who was hired. Group C still has 56 of 160 shortlisted, a rate of 35%. Group D now has 13 of 40 shortlisted.

parts.question: What share of Group D is shortlisted now? Give a percentage to one decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 13 by Group D's 40 applicants.

byKey.count: You read the count, 13, as a percentage. Divide it by 40.
byKey.old: That was the rate before retraining. Use the new count, 13.

explain.text: $13 / 40 = 0.325$, so 32.5% of Group D is shortlisted now.

parts.question: Using Group D's new rate from part 1 and Group C's 35%, how many percentage points apart are they now? Give one decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the new rates.

byKey.old-gap: That was the gap before retraining. Use Group D's new rate.
byKey.counts: You subtracted the counts. Compare rates.

explain.text: The rates are now 35% and 32.5%, which is 2.5 percentage points apart, down from 20.

parts.question: Why did changing what the screener learned from shrink the gap found in part 2?

options.text: A model repeats the pattern in its examples, and the new examples no longer carry the old gap
The network became bigger during the retraining, so it now judges every applicant more fairly
options.why: Nothing says the network grew. The examples changed.

options.text: It was luck: the same screener trained twice will give quite different answers each time
options.why: A gap of 20 points shrinking to 2.5 after a change of data is not luck.

options.text: The group label was removed from every CV, so the screener could no longer see it at all
options.why: Nothing says a label was removed. The target it learned from changed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what changed between the two trainings.

explain.text: A model learns what its examples show. Past hires carried a gap; who meets the requirements does not, since both groups meet them in the same share. So the learned gap shrank.

parts.question: Using the retrained screener from part 3, the firm now wants every applicant's CV pasted into a public chatbot as a second opinion. Which rule from l9 to l11 applies first?

options.text: Personal data stays out of outside tools unless an approved tool and the policy allow it
Check the chatbot's output by calling the applicants back
options.why: Calling back is the rule for payment requests (l11). The first problem is the CVs leaving the firm.

options.text: Test the chatbot's opinions across groups, and then paste the CVs as planned
options.why: Testing across groups matters, but the CVs must not leave the firm first.

options.text: No rule: CVs are written to be read by others
options.why: They were sent to this firm for this job, not to an outside tool.

feedback.correct: Names, contact details and histories are personal data. They stay in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is in a CV.

explain.text: A CV holds names, contact details and work histories: personal data. Pasting them into a public tool sends them outside the firm, so the l9 rule comes first; check your employer's policy and the law where you work.

items.prose: The firm now rewards its screener when a shortlisted candidate accepts an interview. It wanted good hires; it measured accepted interviews.

parts.question: Which is the measure, and which is the meaning?

options.text: Measured: interviews accepted. Meant: good hires.
Measured: good hires. Meant: interviews accepted.
options.why: That is the wrong way round. Interviews are counted; good hires are the aim.

options.text: They are the same thing
options.why: Many accepted interviews can still lead to poor hires.

options.text: Neither: the screener has no goal
options.why: It is trained towards a reward, which acts as its goal.

feedback.correct: Interviews are the measure; good hires are the meaning.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is counted and what is wanted.

explain.text: The firm counts accepted interviews because good hires are hard to measure quickly. Accepted interviews stand in for good hires.

parts.question: Given the measure and meaning from part 1, what might the screener learn?

options.text: To shortlist people likely to say yes, not the people best for the job
To shortlist exactly the people best for the job
options.why: That was meant, but the reward pays for acceptances, which are easier to raise.

options.text: To shortlist nobody
To shortlist everyone
options.why: That is possible, but the cheaper route is choosing people likely to say yes.

feedback.correct: It raises acceptances, which need not mean better hires.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the cheap way to raise the measure.

explain.text: The screener earns its reward when people accept, so it learns to pick people likely to accept. That may not be who is best for the job: measured, not meant.

parts.question: A shortlisted candidate gets an email "from the firm" asking for a £50 fee to book the interview from part 2. What should she do?

options.text: Check with the firm through its own website or a number she already has, and pay nothing yet
Pay the fee, since the interview itself is real and she wants the job
options.why: The interview may be real; the fee request may not be. Check first.

options.text: Reply to the email to ask whether it is genuine
Pay if the email has no spelling mistakes
options.why: Fluent writing is cheap. It proves nothing.

feedback.correct: Check through a channel she already trusts, and pay nothing until then.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which channel the sender cannot control.

explain.text: A fee to book an interview is a payment request, a classic sign. She checks through the firm's own website or a known number, which the sender does not control.
